strengths: Genuinely novel and timely direction: extending the PFN synthetic-prior paradigm from single tables to relational databases with a three-stage generative prior (schema → structure → content) is a sensible and well-motivated contribution, and the paper convincingly argues why conditional generators (SDV, ClavaDDPM, etc.) cannot serve this role.

The core experimental design is fair in an important way: all single-table foundation baselines are given the exact same DFS-linearized inputs as RDB-PFN, so the comparison isolates the modeling/prior contribution rather than feature engineering; the appendix (B.1–B.3) documents baseline configurations in unusual detail, including favorable treatment of competitors (e.g., best Griffin checkpoint per task) and honest discussion of why RT cannot be compared fairly.

The 2.6M-parameter model with 3x–8x faster inference is a real practical contribution, and the efficiency analysis (Table 10, Figure 2) explicitly accounts for hidden ensembling costs of baselines rather than comparing against misleading numbers.

Extensive raw results across 5 context sizes, 19 tasks, 10 seeds, and 23 single-table datasets are provided in the appendix, and the RQ2 'specialization gap' analysis is honest about where the model trails specialized tabular foundation models.

The completeness/expressivity appendix (D.1–D.3.3) is carefully written, with an explicit roadmap mapping the three high-level design principles onto formal assumptions, and implementation details (training curriculum, feature standardization, temporal vocabulary) are specific enough to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'SOTA RDB few-shot performance' is not supported by the paper's own raw numbers. From Tables 4–8, RDB-PFN's average AUC is essentially at parity with TabPFNv2 (0.6517 vs 0.6557 at N=64, 0.6942 vs 0.6967 at N=256, 0.7245 vs 0.7238 at N=1024) — TabPFNv2 actually wins at two of five context sizes. Differences of <0.005 AUC are well within plausible seed noise, yet no significance tests or per-task variance is reported. The aggregate 'normalized score' figures (Fig. 3) visually amplify these tiny margins. The abstract's claims of 'outperforming' baselines and the 'Prior > Scale' contribution therefore overstate the evidence.

Because baselines receive the same DFS features and nearly match RDB-PFN, the paper's key thesis — that a relational prior provides an inductive bias 'that cannot be efficiently replicated simply by scaling up generic tabular data' — is only weakly supported. RQ3's evidence for this is a qualitative correlation-heatmap comparison (Figure 5); no ablation quantifies how much the relational prior (vs. the two-stage curriculum, feature standardization, or added data volume) drives the small gains.

The 'first RDB foundation model trained purely via synthetic data' framing is contestable: the schema prior (LayerDAG) is pre-trained on real-world schemas (Spider, BIRD) per Appendix C.1.1, and concurrent work (RT, Griffin) is explicitly discussed as zero-shot relational models, so the 'first' claim needs careful qualification rather than assertion.

The theoretical contribution is largely cosmetic: Theorem D.6/D.14/D.22/D.23 reduce to standard measurable-sampler/universal-approximation arguments (Lemma D.5 plus chain rule), and the auxiliary assumptions (typewise conditional independence D.8, feature-type ordering D.7, deterministic PKs D.16) assume away most of the actual difficulty of relational distributions. The theorem does not constrain or explain the empirical behavior.

Scope limitations are significant and only partly acknowledged: binary classification only (multi-class/regression 'reserved for future work'), fixed feature width of 30 columns with random subsampling of DFS features (which may discard informative aggregates), and evaluation restricted to small few-shot contexts (≤1024) on a single downstream metric (ROC-AUC).

Presentation and reproducibility issues: the abstract ends with 'The code is available at' followed by no URL; Appendix C.1.2 contains a verbatim duplicated paragraph; Griffin comparison covers only a subset of tasks; and key training details (pre-training compute in GPU-hours, inference latency measurement conditions) are incompletely specified. Combined with near-parity results, independent verification of the headline claims would be difficult.

The RT comparison is dropped entirely on fairness grounds, which is defensible, but leaves the paper without any comparison against the strongest recent native relational approach on its own protocol, weakening the 'genuine foundation model' positioning.

strengths: The problem is timely and well-motivated: extending the PFN/synthetic-prior paradigm from single tables to relational databases is a genuine gap, and the three-stage prior decomposition (schema → structure → content) is a sensible design.

The paper is transparent about several methodological caveats, e.g., it explicitly discusses why a strictly fair comparison with RT (Ranjan et al., 2025) was not possible and how the Griffin comparison was approximated.

The evaluation spans 19 tasks from two established benchmarks (4DBInfer, RelBench) with multiple context sizes, 10 seeds, and a broad baseline suite (TabPFN v2/v2.5, TabICL, Mitra, LimiX, XGBoost, RF, AutoGluon), and raw per-task numbers are provided in the appendix.
Implementation details (Appendix C) and a completeness proof (Appendix D) are provided, giving more procedural detail than many comparable submissions.
weaknesses: The central headline results are not supported by the raw numbers. In the appendix tables, RDB-PFN's average advantage over strong baselines is within ~0.001–0.005 AUC at most context sizes (e.g., N=1024: RDB-PFN 0.7245 vs TabPFNv2 0.7238; N=512: 0.7102 vs 0.7093), and at N=64/128 RDB-PFN actually trails TabPFNv2, LimiX16m, and TabICLv1. No statistical significance tests, win/loss counts, or per-task analyses substantiate the claims of 'Single-Model Dominance' and 'SOTA RDB Few-Shot Performance'.

The claim that the model is 'trained purely on synthetic data' is inaccurate: the schema generator (LayerDAG) is pre-trained on a small corpus of real-world database schemas (Spider, BIRD) (Appendix C.1.1). This directly contradicts the abstract's core selling point and undermines the 'solving scarcity purely via synthetic data' contribution.

The theory is essentially vacuous. Theorem D.23 'universality' follows from assuming the target family already factorizes in exactly the proposed form, assuming each stage's model class is dense, and applying the chain rule plus standard Borel-space randomization lemmas. The assumptions (D.7–D.12, D.16–D.20) largely restate the conclusion; the result provides no insight about whether the practical generator covers real-world relational distributions.

The abstract claims the code is available, but the URL is empty. Reproducibility is therefore unverified: no code, no released synthetic-data generator, and several key hyperparameters (candidate size M, feedback magnitude, mixing ratios) are unspecified.

The model operates at a fixed 600 rows × 30 columns with DFS features randomly downsampled from 60–90 generated columns. How this handles wide schemas (e.g., Rel-trial with 140 columns) and whether the random downsampling discards informative features is neither explained nor ablated.

Critical ablations are missing: no ablation of the two-stage curriculum, the temporal vocabulary, the hybrid preferential-attachment sampling, or the relational prior vs. simply more single-table data at matched compute. RQ3's evidence is limited to qualitative correlation-heatmap inspection (Figure 5), which is weak support for the 'Relational Prior' causal claim.

The scope is restricted to binary classification with binarized multi-class targets and ROC-AUC only, while many tasks hover near chance (AUC ≈ 0.5 for Diginetica, Outbrain, etc.), inflating the apparent uniformity of results and limiting practical significance. Regression and multi-class are deferred to future work.

Efficiency claims are overstated: inference time is 34s vs 36s for TabICL-Lite (Table 10) — a negligible difference — yet Figure 2 asserts RDB-PFN 'dominates the efficiency landscape' with '3x–8x faster inference', conflating single-estimator and ensemble configurations.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: a verbatim duplicated sentence in Appendix C.1.2, an incomplete code link, and heavily aggregated/normalized plots (Figures 2–3) that obscure the marginal and mixed raw results documented in the appendix.

Classical baselines received 'lightweight, budgeted hyperparameter optimization' without specifying the tuning budget, data, or protocol, raising fairness and potential leakage concerns in the few-shot setting.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: extending the PFN synthetic-pretraining paradigm to relational databases addresses a genuine gap, and the proposed Relational Prior (schema generation via LayerDAG, selective SCM for FK structure, hierarchical GNN content generation) is a reasonable and creative instantiation of the Schema→Structure→Content decomposition.

The 'Prior > Scale' hypothesis is testable and the experimental design is thoughtful: all single-table foundation-model baselines are given the exact same DFS-linearized features, and both ensemble and single-estimator configurations are reported, which strengthens fairness of the architectural comparison.

Very good transparency in the appendix: complete raw per-task results for all context sizes (Tables 4–8), explicit baseline configurations including deviations (e.g., disabling SVD preprocessing for LimiX), and an honest negative control showing RDB-PFN trails specialized single-table models on flat tabular data (Figure 4, Table 9).
Strong efficiency profile: 2.6M parameters and fast inference, with clear latency/data comparisons (Table 10, Figure 2).
The completeness proof effort (Appendix D) is carefully organized and clearly distinguishes main-text assumptions from the operational proof assumptions.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'Single-Model Dominance' is not fully supported by the raw results: at context size 64 RDB-PFN's average (0.6517) is below TabPFNv2 (0.6557) and LimiX16m (0.6575), and at N=128 it roughly ties the best baselines (0.6688 vs 0.6692 TabICLv1). The advantage emerges mainly at larger contexts, which should be stated more precisely rather than as blanket dominance.

No statistical significance testing is reported. Averages across the 19 tasks differ by very small margins (e.g., 0.7245 vs 0.7238 at N=1024), so the central empirical claim needs uncertainty quantification at the aggregate level (e.g., paired tests over tasks) beyond per-task seed variance.

The universality result (Theorem D.23) is essentially circular: it assumes each stage family is dense in the admissible class and then concludes the composite is dense; given Lemma D.5's chain-rule construction, the theorem has limited technical depth and does not meaningfully validate the practical generator.

Comparison against graph-based RDB models is weak: the Griffin comparison uses an idealized best-checkpoint-per-task 'ensemble' on only a subset of tasks, and the RT comparison is explicitly abandoned ('unable to establish a strictly fair comparison protocol'), despite the abstract claiming outperformance of graph-based baselines. Standard per-task fine-tuned GNN baselines from 4DBInfer/RelBench are absent from the main results.

Binary classification only; multi-class and regression are deferred, which limits the scope of the 'foundation model' claim, and the framework is evaluated only up to N=1024 in-context samples, well below industrial-scale usage.

Reproducibility concerns: the code URL in the abstract is missing/empty, and key details (how the temporal split semantics of RelBench tasks interact with uniformly random context sampling, exact normalized-score aggregation) are underspecified.

Missing ablations tying performance to prior design choices: the Hybrid Sampling strategy, temporal vocabulary, and feedback mechanism (Appendix C) are described but never ablated against final task performance, so 'Prior > Scale' rests on the single comparison against single-table priors rather than on causal evidence about which prior components matter.

Presentation issues: duplicated sentence in Appendix C.1.2, a dense and hard-to-parse Figure 1, and occasional overclaiming (e.g., 'first relational foundation model' sits uneasily alongside the cited Griffin and RT).

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and timely: extending the PFN/synthetic-prior paradigm from single tables to relational databases via an unconditional relational prior (schema generation with LayerDAG, selective SCM for FK/link generation, GNN-based content completion) directly addresses the genuine data-scarcity bottleneck in the RDB domain.

The experimental suite is unusually thorough for this area: 19 tasks across 4DBInfer/RelBench with 10 seeds and multiple context sizes, full raw per-task tables (Tables 6-30), PR-AUC robustness checks for imbalanced tasks, strengthened classical baselines (tuned XGBoost, best-quality AutoGluon), fine-tuning and cross-task adaptation studies, chunked-support context scaling, and ablations over both the relational prior and the backbone.

The comparison design is largely fair: single-table foundation models (TabPFNv2.5, TabICL, Mitra, LimiX) are given the exact same DFS-linearized features, and both ensemble and single-estimator variants are reported; protocol differences with Griffin and RT are discussed candidly in Appendix B.3 rather than glossed over.

An honest limitations section explicitly scopes the contribution (binary classification, few-shot global support set, DFS-based interface), and ablations confirm that each prior component (schema generator, link mechanism, temporal component, locality) contributes.

The pairing of a sophisticated relational prior with a deliberately simple 'linearize-and-attend' backbone, plus the RDBPFN-Single ablation isolating the relational pre-training stage, is a clean experimental design for attributing gains to the prior rather than architecture.
weaknesses: The headline performance claim ('explicitly outperforms all single-table baselines') is weaker than the evidence supports. In the raw tables, margins are small (~0.005-0.01 average ROC-AUC at context 1024) and sometimes reversed: at context 64, RDB-PFN (0.6517) trails TabPFNv2 (0.6557) and LimiX16m (0.6575) on average. No statistical significance tests are reported despite 10 seeds, so the 'Single-Model Dominance' and 'clearly surpasses' language overstates what the data shows.

The claimed 'first RDB foundation model' positioning is contestable given Griffin and RT, and those native relational models are excluded from same-protocol comparison with protocol-mismatch justifications. The Griffin comparison uses an idealized per-task best-checkpoint selection, which partially mitigates but does not eliminate this gap.

The universality theory (Appendix E, Theorem E.23) adds limited value: the proof reduces to the standard measurable-sampler lemma plus chain-rule factorization under strong, somewhat artificial assumptions (E.7-E.12, E.16-E.20). The gap between these idealized assumptions and the practical neural generators (attention-based selective SCM) is not bridged, so the theorem functions more as a framing device than a guarantee.

The setting is deliberately narrow: binary classification only (multiclass via one-vs-rest is claimed but never evaluated), a single global support-set ICL protocol, fixed 600x30 input shape, and heavy reliance on DFS as the relational interface. The DFS sensitivity analysis (Table 4) itself shows large swings (e.g., Diginetica 0.5225 vs 0.7004 between DFS-1 and DFS-2), meaning conclusions are partly contingent on a non-optimal, hand-chosen linearization.

Reproducibility is undermined by a placeholder code link in the abstract ('The code is available at .'), and several implementation details needed for reproduction (e.g., how the prior generator's neural modules are trained, exact pre-training loss) are spread thin or deferred. Some presentation issues (low-resolution Figures 2-3, encoding artifacts in references) further detract.

The RQ2 result shows RDB-PFN trails specialized single-table foundation models on the standard tabular benchmark, so the practical benefit over simply running an existing TFM on DFS features rests on the small average margins in RQ1 rather than a categorical advantage.

strengths: The core idea—extending the PFN synthetic-pretraining paradigm from single tables to relational databases via a decomposed Schema→Structure→Content prior—is timely and well-motivated, addressing a genuine gap between relational learning and tabular foundation models.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for a paper in this space: 19 tasks across 4DBInfer/RelBench, multiple context sizes (64–1024), 10 seeds, PR-AUC robustness checks, fine-tuning and chunked-context scaling analyses, and full per-task raw results in the appendix (Tables 6–30).

The ablation study (relational prior components, backbone attention design, model size, DFS configuration) is systematic and provides useful evidence about which design choices matter, including the honest finding that the LayerDAG schema prior gives only 'a slight but consistent improvement'.

The paper is candid in places: it acknowledges the constrained setting (binary classification, fixed-size tasks, global support set), reports that RDB-PFN trails specialized single-table TFMs on single-table benchmarks, and treats Griffin/RT as protocol-incompatible references rather than fabricating direct comparisons.
The lightweight 0.7M-parameter model and the DFS-linearize-and-attend design choice (isolating prior contribution from architecture) is a sensible experimental strategy.
weaknesses: The headline empirical gains are marginal and fragile. In the raw tables, RDB-PFN's average ROC-AUC advantage over the best tabular foundation models is often ~0.001–0.013 (e.g., 0.7245 vs. 0.7238 for TabPFNv2 at N=1024; at N=64 several baselines including LimiX16m and TabPFNv2 actually exceed RDB-PFN), yet the paper claims RDB-PFN 'clearly surpasses all baselines'. No statistical significance tests are reported, and aggregated 'normalized score' curves obscure the small, inconsistent per-task differences.

The 'trained purely via synthetic data' claim is overstated. The schema generator (LayerDAG) is pre-trained on real-world schema corpora (Spider, 4DBInfer), and the structural generator uses learnable projections whose training procedure is never clearly explained. How the prior's MLPs/attention modules acquire their parameters without real data is a genuine soundness and clarity gap at the heart of the paper's positioning.

The missing direct comparison with RT (Ranjan et al., 2025), the most relevant recent zero-shot relational model, materially weakens the 'first genuine RDB foundation model' claim. The protocol-difference justification is reasonable but the paper compensates only with a same-protocol comparison against Griffin on a subset of tasks, not against RT under any shared setting.

The theoretical contribution is thin. The 'universality' result (Theorem E.23) follows almost immediately from chain-rule factorization, measurable-sampling lemmas, and universal approximation, and only holds within the assumption-defined family. The assumptions (typewise conditional independence, mechanism sharing, bounded-hop locality) essentially restate the architecture's structure, making the theorem close to circular rather than a substantive expressivity guarantee.

The efficiency narrative is partially confounded: the 3.0–6.7x inference speedup is 'largely due to avoiding expensive default ensembling' (the paper's own admission), and against single-estimator Lite variants the gap nearly vanishes (e.g., 34s vs. TabICL-Lite's 36s). Framing this as a foundation-model efficiency achievement overstates the contribution.

Scope limitations substantially undercut the 'foundation model' framing: binary classification only (one-vs-rest for multiclass), fixed ~600-row tasks, capped context of 1024 (extended only via costly chunked ensembling), and no regression, ranking, or temporal-horizon tasks, which are common in RelBench.

The ablations are run on a heavily reduced training budget (20k RDBs vs. ~1.2M in the full pipeline), so conclusions about prior components may not transfer to the final model; this discrepancy is disclosed but not analyzed.

Prior work positioning relies on arXiv preprints (many from 2025) and several cited baselines' checkpoints/checkpoint names are unverifiable; the reproducibility of the prior-generation pipeline, which involves multiple learned modules with unspecified training details, is questionable despite the code link.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly positioned: RDBs lack internet-scale public pre-training corpora, so the PFN paradigm of learning from an infinite synthetic prior is a natural and original transfer to the relational setting. The three-stage prior (Schema via LayerDAG, Structure via Selective SCM, Content via hierarchical GNN SCM) is a concrete, reusable contribution, and the paper convincingly argues why conditional generators (SDV/ClavaDDPM/RelDiff) cannot serve this purpose.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: 19 real relational tasks from 4DBInfer/RelBench, multiple context sizes (64-1024) with 10 seeds, single-table transfer checks, PR-AUC for imbalanced tasks, fine-tuning and cross-task adaptation, chunked-support scaling, extensive prior and backbone ablations, and full raw per-task tables in the appendix (Tables 6-30). This level of transparency substantially supports reproducibility of the reported numbers.

The baseline protocol is mostly fair and carefully justified: single-table foundation models (TabPFNv2.5, TabICL, Mitra, LimiX) receive the exact same DFS-linearized features, both default and single-estimator variants are reported, and classical baselines (XGBoost, AutoGluon, RF) are strengthened with budgeted tuning rather than run with weak defaults.

The limitations discussion is honest and specific: the binary-classification head, the constrained few-shot global-support ICL protocol, the acknowledged 'specialization gap' on single-table benchmarks, and the framing of Griffin/RT as protocol-incompatible references rather than direct baselines are all clearly disclosed rather than hidden.
The efficiency analysis (0.7M parameters, ~2M synthetic datasets, 3.0-6.7x faster inference) with raw numbers in Table 5 substantiates the 'prior > scale' claim in a verifiable way.
weaknesses: The headline claim of outperforming single-table foundation models is weaker than the raw data suggests. In the appendix tables, average ROC-AUC differences are small and inconsistent across context sizes: e.g., at context 256 RDBPFN averages 0.6942 vs TabPFNv2 0.6967, at 1024 it is 0.7245 vs TabPFNv2.5 0.7200, and under PR-AUC at context 64 RDBPFN (0.5191) is essentially tied with TabPFNv2.5 (0.5191) and loses on several tasks. The abstract's 'outperforming' framing is not consistently supported; error bars on the aggregated curves and per-task significance analysis are not provided.

No direct comparison with native relational foundation models is achieved. Griffin and RT are excluded as same-protocol baselines with reasonable arguments, but this means the paper's central claim of a superior RDB foundation model rests only on tabular models given DFS features plus a best-checkpoint 'idealized' Griffin reference. Given that RT is explicitly described as zero-shot with a different protocol, a unified evaluation under a common protocol would have substantially strengthened the contribution.

The theoretical contribution is largely decorative. Theorem E.23's density conclusion follows from assumed density of each stage family (conditions (i)-(iii) are assumed, not established for the actual architectures), and the completeness proofs are chain-rule plus standard randomization/universal-approximation arguments. The assumptions in the appendix (feature-type ordering, typewise conditional independence, deterministic PKs) go well beyond the three main-text principles, so the theorem does not validate the implemented generator in a meaningful sense.

A code link is promised in the abstract ('The code is available at .') but the URL is missing, undermining the reproducibility claim; the schema generator is also trained on a small corpus of real schemas (Spider/4DBInfer), which slightly weakens the 'purely synthetic' narrative and deserves more prominent discussion.

The evaluation scope is narrow relative to the 'foundation model' framing: only binary classification, fixed task sizes (downsampling to 600 rows during pre-training, N<=1024 ICL), and a global shared support set that does not reflect how relational supervision is typically distributed. The strictly fair comparison thus occurs in a regime constructed to favor ICL methods, and the paper's own ablations (D.4) acknowledge that the DFS interface is non-optimal and task-sensitive.
Single-table verification downsamples all datasets to N=1000, a regime known to favor PFN-style methods, making the RQ2 comparison less informative than it appears.
